The global energy sector is undergoing a profound transformation driven by the urgent need to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, increase energy efficiency, and enhance grid resilience.

Among renewable energy sources, solar photovoltaic (PV) technology has emerged as a cornerstone of the sustainable energy transition due to its scalability, declining costs, and versatility of deployment ranging from residential rooftops to utility-scale solar farms [1].

However, the rapid growth of PV installations has brought new challenges in ensuring system reliability, reducing downtime, and minimizing operational costs. Unlike conventional power plants that rely on centralized maintenance procedures, distributed PV systems often operate under highly variable environmental and load conditions, making their components vulnerable to unpredictable failures.

At the center of this challenge lies the solar inverter, a vital device that not only converts direct current (DC) into alternating current (AC) but also regulates power quality, harmonics, and grid compliance. Solar inverters act as the "heart" of PV systems, continuously interacting with both the generation side and the grid side to maintain system stability. Yet, studies consistently report that inverters are the most failure-prone components of PV infrastructure, accounting for more than half of unscheduled maintenance events [2]. This high failure rate poses significant risks to energy yield, investment returns, and the long-term viability of large-scale PV adoption.

The complexity of inverter failures is amplified by the interplay of multiple stressors such as temperature fluctuations, dust accumulation, semiconductor aging, and grid disturbances. Unlike mechanical equipment, inverter failures often manifest through subtle electrical and thermal anomalies rather than easily visible physical degradation. Consequently, conventional maintenance approaches, such as scheduled replacements or reactive repairs, prove inefficient and costly. These approaches either overestimate component wear, leading to premature part replacements, or underestimate failures, resulting in unexpected downtime and costly repairs.

In response to these limitations, the research community and industry have increasingly turned to predictive maintenance (PdM), a strategy that uses real-time data, advanced analytics, and AI-driven models to anticipate failures before they occur. Predictive maintenance not only minimizes downtime and repair costs but also extends the lifespan of critical components, thereby improving overall system efficiency and resilience [3]. While PdM has been successfully applied in manufacturing, aviation, and industrial automation, its application to solar inverter systems remains relatively underexplored. This research gap forms the central motivation for the present study.

The accelerated deployment of photovoltaic (PV) systems worldwide underscores the critical role of solar energy in transitioning to a sustainable, low-carbon energy future. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), global solar PV capacity exceeded 1 TW in 2023, with projections suggesting that solar will become the dominant source of electricity by 2050 [1].

Central to these systems are solar inverters, which convert direct current (DC) generated by PV modules into alternating current (AC) suitable for grid integration and end-user consumption.

Inverters also regulate voltage and frequency, provide grid support functions, and ensure compliance with increasingly stringent interconnection standards.

Despite their importance, solar inverters remain one of the most failure-prone components of PV systems. Studies indicate that inverter-related faults account for more than 50% of unscheduled maintenance events in utility-scale solar farms [2]. These failures arise from a combination of factors, including semiconductor aging, thermal cycling, power fluctuations, dust accumulation, and adverse environmental conditions. The resulting outages not only reduce energy yield but also increase operational and maintenance (O&M) costs, posing a major barrier to widespread PV adoption.

Traditional maintenance strategies, such as corrective (reactive) maintenance or preventive (scheduled) maintenance, are insufficient in this context. Corrective maintenance leads to extended downtime and high repair costs, while preventive maintenance often replaces components prematurely, leading to wasted resources. Consequently, there is growing interest in predictive maintenance (PdM) approaches that leverage advanced sensing, data analytics, and artificial intelligence (AI) to forecast faults before they occur. By predicting the remaining useful life (RUL) of critical components, PdM enables condition-based interventions, ensuring reliability while minimizing cost.

Although predictive maintenance has been widely studied in industrial systems such as rotating machinery and manufacturing lines [3], its application to solar inverter systems remains underdeveloped. Existing inverter monitoring solutions primarily rely on threshold-based alarms or simple statistical models, which lack the sophistication to detect complex, nonlinear fault signatures. Furthermore, most field-deployed monitoring platforms are limited to real-time fault detection rather than predictive forecasting. Solar inverters present unique challenges for predictive maintenance. Unlike mechanical assets, their failures often involve nonlinear interactions between electrical, thermal, and environmental variables. For example, capacitor degradation manifests through subtle shifts in impedance and harmonic distortion, while semiconductor wear-out can lead to temperature spikes under partial load. Capturing and interpreting such multidimensional data requires machine learning and deep learning approaches capable of modeling nonlinear, time-dependent relationships. Moreover, the dynamic operating conditions of PV systems, driven by diurnal solar variability, weather fluctuations, and grid disturbances, make it difficult to distinguish between normal variations and early fault precursors.

Therefore, the research problem addressed in this study is the lack of advanced AI-driven predictive maintenance frameworks for solar inverter systems that can (i) detect hidden anomalies in operational data, (ii) accurately predict component degradation trends, and (iii) provide actionable maintenance schedules to maximize inverter uptime and reliability.

To address these challenges, this paper proposes an AI-driven predictive maintenance framework specifically tailored for solar inverter systems. The framework integrates real-time sensor data, historical maintenance records, and simulated fault scenarios to train machine learning models capable of detecting and predicting inverter faults. The methodology involves four major stages: The proposed framework leverages MATLAB/Simulink for system-level simulation of inverter behavior under variable conditions, while Python-based AI libraries are used to implement learning algorithms. This hybrid approach ensures both the accuracy of physical modeling and the adaptability of AI-driven insights.

The primary contributions of this work are as follows:

1. Development of an AI-based predictive maintenance framework for solar inverter systems that integrates real-time data analytics with advanced machine learning algorithms.

2. Design and implementation of feature engineering techniques that capture both electrical and thermal characteristics of inverter faults.

5.

Comprehensive comparison of AI models, including supervised (e.g., support vector machines, random forests) and deep learning (e.g., CNN, LSTM) approaches, to identify the most effective predictive algorithms for inverter systems.

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section II reviews existing research on predictive maintenance, solar inverter reliability, AI-based fault detection, and RUL prediction methods. Section III presents the proposed system architecture and methodology, including inverter modeling, data-driven analytics, and AI workflow integration. Section IV discusses simulation results, comparative analysis of AI models, and performance validation. Section V concludes the paper with key findings, practical implications, and directions for future research.

subsection: A. Reliability of Solar Inverter Systems
text: Solar inverters are widely recognized as the most failure-prone component in PV installations, with studies indicating that inverter failures account for nearly 50% of downtime events in large-scale PV plants [4]. Common issues include capacitor degradation, semiconductor aging, thermal cycling, and dust-induced derating [5]. Preventive maintenance strategies, such as periodic replacements, have been proposed to mitigate failures, but these approaches often lead to premature component replacement and elevated lifecycle costs [6]. Recent studies emphasize that inverter reliability can be improved through condition monitoring and advanced diagnostics, but traditional monitoring platforms are limited to threshold alarms rather than predictive insights [7]. This underscores the need for advanced AI-driven frameworks capable of capturing nonlinear fault patterns in inverter operations.

subsection: B. Predictive Maintenance in Power Electronics
text: Predictive maintenance (PdM) has been applied extensively across industrial machinery, transportation, and manufacturing systems [8]. In the domain of power electronics, early efforts focused on statistical degradation models and thermal stress analysis [9]. More recent works employ physics-of-failure (PoF) approaches, modeling wear-out mechanisms of semiconductors and capacitors to estimate remaining useful life (RUL) [10]. While effective, PoF approaches are computationally demanding and require detailed component-level parameters often unavailable in real-world settings. Data-driven PdM, using machine learning and deep learning, offers a promising alternative by leveraging operational data to identify degradation trends without requiring exhaustive physical models [11]. However, research on predictive maintenance specifically tailored to solar inverter systems remains limited, creating an opportunity for integrating AI methods into PV asset management.

subsection: C. AI for Fault Detection in Solar Inverters
text:
Artificial intelligence has shown great potential in enhancing fault detection capabilities for inverter systems. Machine learning algorithms, such as support vector machines (SVM) and random forests, have been used to classify inverter faults based on electrical signatures [12].

Deep learning methods, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), extend this capability by automatically extracting features from raw sensor data [13]. Hybrid methods combining signal processing techniques with AI models have demonstrated improvements in detecting early-stage inverter anomalies, particularly under fluctuating solar irradiance and grid disturbances [14]. Despite these advances, many of these studies focus on fault classification rather than predictive forecasting, limiting their application in maintenance planning.

Estimating the remaining useful life of inverter components is a critical challenge for predictive maintenance. Traditional methods employ statistical approaches, such as Weibull analysis and proportional hazard models, to estimate RUL [15]. Recent research has increasingly adopted machine learning models, such as LSTM networks and gated recurrent units (GRUs), which are well-suited for capturing temporal dependencies in inverter degradation data [16]. These models have shown strong predictive performance in rotating machinery and battery systems, but their application in inverter systems is still emerging [17]. Incorporating RUL estimation into solar inverter maintenance can provide actionable scheduling insights, reducing downtime while optimizing lifecycle management.

subsection: E. Research Gap and Positioning of This Work
text: Although prior studies have demonstrated significant advances in inverter reliability modeling, predictive maintenance in power electronics, AI-driven fault detection, and RUL estimation, several gaps remain. First, most inverter fault detection systems remain reactive, identifying issues after they occur rather than forecasting them. Second, many existing predictive maintenance frameworks are not specifically designed for solar inverters, which operate under highly dynamic solar and grid conditions. Finally, there is limited integration of simulation-based modeling (e.g., MATLAB/Simulink) with AI-driven predictive analytics, which restricts reproducibility and scalability. This paper addresses these gaps by proposing an AI-driven predictive maintenance framework for solar inverter systems that combines physics-based simulation, data-driven feature extraction, and deep learning models for anomaly detection and RUL prediction. By validating the framework through MATLAB/Simulink and AI co-simulation, this research contributes to bridging the gap between theoretical algorithm design and practical solar inverter maintenance.

The proposed framework for AI-driven predictive maintenance of solar inverter systems is designed as a multi-layered architecture that integrates physical modeling, data processing, machine learning, and decision support. This methodology ensures that both the electrical and thermal behaviors of solar inverters are captured through simulations and subsequently analyzed using artificial intelligence techniques for fault detection and remaining useful life (RUL) prediction.

The architecture is structured into three complementary layers. The first is the physical modeling layer, which uses MATLAB/Simulink to replicate the operational behavior of solar inverters under different environmental and grid conditions. This includes modeling both fault-free scenarios and specific fault conditions, such as capacitor aging, semiconductor degradation, and open-circuit switching faults. The second layer is the data processing layer, where signals generated from the inverter model are collected, filtered, and prepared for further analysis. This stage ensures that raw data is transformed into meaningful inputs for artificial intelligence models. Finally, the third layer is the AI analytics layer, where fault detection, anomaly recognition, and RUL forecasting are carried out using machine learning and deep learning approaches. Together, these three layers form a closed-loop architecture in which simulated and real-world data can be processed to provide actionable maintenance recommendations.

At the foundation of the framework lies a detailed inverter model constructed in MATLAB/Simulink. The photovoltaic subsystem is based on the single-diode equivalent circuit, which accurately captures the nonlinear current-voltage characteristics of solar panels under varying irradiance and temperature. The generated DC power is then regulated by a DC-DC boost converter equipped with a Perturb & Observe (P&O) maximum power point tracking (MPPT) algorithm to ensure that the PV system operates at maximum efficiency.

The boosted DC voltage is supplied to a DC-AC inverter modeled using an insulated-gate bipolar transistor (IGBT) bridge with sinusoidal pulse-width modulation (SPWM). This inverter feeds power into the grid, where performance is monitored in terms of power factor, harmonics, and voltage stability. In addition to electrical behavior, a thermal model is incorporated to simulate temperature variations in switching devices, allowing the study of thermal stress as a precursor to semiconductor failure. Through this modeling approach, both normal operating data and data from fault scenarios-such as IGBT short-circuits, capacitor degradation, and overheating-are generated.

These datasets provide the basis for training and validating AI models. Figure 2

subsection: C. Data Preprocessing and Feature Engineering
text:
The raw signals produced during simulation contain noise and redundancy, which makes preprocessing a critical step. Data is first smoothed using filtering techniques, such as moving averages and wavelet filters, to remove measurement noise. Normalization is then applied to scale different features consistently, ensuring that variables with larger ranges do not dominate the learning process. Finally, the data is segmented into time windows to facilitate real-time prediction of faults and degradation.

Feature engineering is particularly important for translating raw inverter signals into indicators of health and degradation. Statistical features, such as mean, variance, kurtosis, and skewness, capture deviations in current and voltage signals. Frequency-domain features are extracted through Fourier transforms, enabling analysis of harmonic distortion and spectral entropy as markers of inverter stress. Time-frequency features, including wavelet packet energy and short-time Fourier transforms, provide localized information about transient disturbances. subsection: D. AI Models for Fault Detection and Prediction
text:
The artificial intelligence component of the framework integrates multiple models for different predictive tasks. For fault classification, supervised learning models such as support vector machines (SVM), random forests, and gradient boosting are employed. These algorithms can learn from labeled datasets and distinguish between normal and faulty operating states.

In addition to classification, anomaly detection methods such as autoencoders and one-class SVMs are used to recognize deviations from baseline operation without requiring explicit fault labels. This makes them particularly useful for identifying early degradation stages that have not yet developed into observable failures.

For long-term forecasting, deep learning models such as long short-term memory (LSTM) networks and gated recurrent units (GRUs) are applied. These recurrent neural networks excel at learning temporal dependencies in time-series data, making them ideal for predicting degradation trends and estimating the RUL of inverter components. Model performance is assessed using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score for classification tasks, and root mean square error (RMSE)

for RUL estimation.

The outputs of the AI models are consolidated in a decision-support module, which provides actionable insights for operations and maintenance teams. Fault alerts are issued in real time,

identifying not only the presence of a fault but also its specific type, such as capacitor degradation or semiconductor overheating. RUL predictions provide quantitative estimates of how long components can operate before requiring replacement. Based on this information, optimized maintenance schedules are generated that minimize downtime and reduce costs compared to rigid time-based maintenance. This decision support enables solar plant operators to move from reactive to proactive maintenance, improving reliability and efficiency.

To ensure robustness, the proposed framework is validated in three stages. First, simulation-based validation is performed using data generated in MATLAB/Simulink, which allows systematic testing of different fault scenarios. Second, external validation is conducted using real-world datasets from inverter manufacturers and field-deployed PV systems, ensuring generalizability. Finally, comparative benchmarking is carried out against conventional threshold-based alarms and statistical degradation models. These comparisons demonstrate the superiority of the AI-driven approach in terms of fault detection accuracy and predictive reliability.

The first stage of evaluation focused on the accuracy of AI models in classifying inverter faults.

Inverter failures often manifest in subtle deviations in current, voltage, or harmonic patterns, which makes accurate classification essential for predictive maintenance. Traditional methods such as threshold alarms detect faults only after they occur and often result in false positives under fluctuating solar irradiance. In contrast, AI-based models can leverage complex patterns in data to identify early fault signatures. Support Vector Machines (SVM) were initially tested due to their robustness in handling binary classification tasks. SVMs achieved satisfactory accuracy when differentiating between normal and faulty states but struggled in multi-class classification, such as distinguishing capacitor degradation from IGBT short-circuit faults. Random Forests (RF), by contrast, provided higher robustness in multi-class problems. By combining multiple decision trees, RF captured nonlinear boundaries between classes and achieved higher fault detection accuracy, especially under diverse operating conditions. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) significantly outperformed both SVM and RF when applied to raw time-series waveform data. By automatically extracting spatial-temporal features, CNNs reduced the reliance on manual feature engineering and showed superior accuracy in detecting simultaneous or overlapping fault signatures.

The second stage of analysis addressed anomaly detection, which plays a critical role in identifying early warning signs of degradation before complete failure occurs. Unlike classification tasks that require labeled data, anomaly detection models learn the normal operating behavior of inverters and flag deviations as potential faults. This is particularly useful in real-world settings where fault labels are scarce or incomplete.

One-class SVMs were initially applied due to their effectiveness in identifying deviations from a baseline operating profile. While they performed reasonably well in detecting large deviations, they often failed to recognize subtle anomalies that precede major failures. Autoencoders, a type of neural network designed for unsupervised learning, provided a more powerful solution. By compressing input signals into a low-dimensional latent space and reconstructing them, autoencoders identified even small deviations between reconstructed and actual signals, making them highly sensitive to early degradation.

Experimental results indicated that autoencoders consistently outperformed one-class SVMs in both sensitivity and precision. Their ability to learn compact, nonlinear representations of inverter signals allowed them to generalize across varying irradiance and temperature conditions. This is crucial because inverter anomalies often manifest differently depending on the external environment.

These findings highlight that anomaly detection using autoencoders provides a practical tool for real-time monitoring of inverters, enabling operators to identify degradation much earlier than with traditional monitoring systems.

A critical aspect of predictive maintenance is the ability to forecast the remaining useful life (RUL) of inverter components such as DC link capacitors, IGBTs, and cooling fans. RUL prediction enables operators to schedule maintenance activities proactively rather than reactively, thus avoiding unexpected failures and unnecessary downtime.

In this study, RUL estimation was carried out using deep learning approaches, specifically Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) and Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) networks. Both are designed to handle temporal dependencies in time-series data, making them well-suited for modeling gradual degradation trends. Results indicated that LSTM networks delivered superior accuracy in modeling long-term dependencies, particularly in capturing the nonlinear degradation trajectories of capacitors subjected to thermal cycling. GRUs, while slightly less accurate, provided faster training times and lower computational requirements, making them attractive for deployment in embedded hardware with limited resources.

Quantitatively, LSTM achieved the lowest root mean square error (RMSE) in RUL prediction compared to GRU and regression-based baselines. This suggests that LSTM is more reliable for applications where long-term accuracy is critical. However, the trade-off in computational cost suggests that GRUs may be preferable in resource-constrained environments, particularly in distributed PV systems where local processing capabilities are limited.

To consolidate the findings, a comparative analysis was conducted across all AI models used in this study. Table 2 summarizes the performance of supervised models (SVM, RF, CNN), unsupervised anomaly detectors (One-Class SVM, Autoencoder), and deep learning models (LSTM, GRU). Each model demonstrated distinct strengths and limitations, suggesting that a hybrid approach may be the most effective strategy for predictive maintenance. This holistic comparison demonstrates the potential of AI-driven predictive maintenance to significantly improve solar inverter reliability while reducing costs. In conclusion, this paper has laid the groundwork for a robust, AI-driven predictive maintenance system tailored for solar inverter applications. By uniting physics-based simulations, machine learning models, and decision-support systems, the framework demonstrates its potential to revolutionize inverter reliability and maintenance strategies. Looking ahead, future research that integrates hybrid AI architectures, real-time IoT deployment, transfer learning, and explainability will be crucial in transforming predictive maintenance from a promising research concept into a mainstream industrial standard. Such advancements will accelerate the global transition toward resilient, cost-effective, and sustainable renewable energy systems.
